nameStory: Gammarus fasciatus gets its scientific name from the Latin word 'gammarus' meaning shrimp or lobster, reflecting its curved, shrimp-like body shape. The species name 'fasciatus' means 'banded,' referring to the subtle striped patterns that sometimes appear across its segments.
description: Gammarus fasciatus is a tiny freshwater crustacean that looks like a miniature shrimp curled on its side. These amphipods (meaning 'different feet') are usually less than half an inch long and have flattened, comma-shaped bodies that appear almost translucent. They're part of the same big family as lobsters and crabs, just much smaller and built for life in streams and ponds. You'll often see them scooting along the bottom or swimming in quick, jerky motions through the water.

idTips.label: Curved body shape
idTips.description: Body is distinctly flattened from side to side and naturally curved like a tiny comma or question mark, especially when at rest

idTips.label: Swimming motion
idTips.description: Moves through water with quick, darting jerks rather than smooth swimming, often tumbling or spinning as it goes

idTips.label: Size and color
idTips.description: About the size of a grain of rice to small pea, typically pale gray, tan, or nearly transparent with a slightly glossy appearance

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Two pairs of long, thread-like antennae that are often longer than the body and constantly twitching as they explore

idTips.label: Side-swimming posture
idTips.description: Always lies on its side when resting, never upright like a typical shrimp, and swims sideways through the water

habitat: Found in clean, cool freshwater streams, springs, and well-oxygenated ponds throughout New England's forested areas. They prefer areas with rocky or gravelly bottoms where they can hide under stones, fallen logs, or among aquatic plants. Look for them in shallow water near the edges of streams or in the clear, slow-moving sections of brooks.

seasonality.spring: Most active as water temperatures warm, often found in large numbers under stones in shallow stream margins. This is when they're easiest to spot as they emerge from winter hiding spots.
seasonality.summer: Continue to be active but may move to deeper, cooler water during hot weather. Look for them in shaded stream sections or springs.
seasonality.fall: Still active and visible, often gathering in areas that will remain unfrozen. Good time to observe them before they seek winter shelter.
seasonality.winter: Remain active under ice in flowing water, though much harder to observe. They don't hibernate but become less active in very cold water.

funFact: These tiny crustaceans are actually living water quality indicators - they're so sensitive to pollution that scientists use their presence to determine if a stream is healthy enough to support trout and other sensitive fish species.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with tiny fish fry or aquatic worms, but the distinctive sideways swimming and comma-shaped resting posture are dead giveaways. Remember: if it swims on its side and looks like a tiny translucent question mark, it's likely a scud.
contextualKnowledge: These creatures are commonly called 'scuds' or 'side-swimmers' by anglers and stream ecologists, terms that are much easier to remember than their scientific name. The name 'scud' comes from an old nautical term meaning to move quickly, perfectly describing their darting swimming style.
compareHints: Gammarus fasciatus is distinguished from its saltwater cousin the Tide-pool Scud by its smaller size and freshwater habitat, while Gammarus mucronatus tends to be slightly larger and more robust. In the field, habitat is your best clue - if you're in freshwater streams or ponds inland, you're almost certainly looking at G. fasciatus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Pointed Scuds are distinguished from their cousin the Tide-pool Scud by their more prominent spines and pointed body segments that give them their name.
Tide-pool scuds differ from their freshwater cousin, the common scud (Gammarus fasciatus), by their tolerance for salt water and slightly more robust build.
